question.leadin: A powerful family that ruled this city included men like Lorezno the Magnificent.
question.text: Name this Italian city once ruled by the Medici family. This city is the most populous one in Tuscany.
question.clue: This city was the site of the Pazzi conspiracy, and much of its art and literature was destroyed in the Bonfire of the Vanities, ordered by the monk Savonarola.

swap.leadin: A palace in this city contains portraits of all of its rulers except one, whose portrait was replaced by a black sheet as punishment for treason.
swap.text: Name this Italian city at the end of the Adriatic Sea which was a merchant republic ruled by doges such as Enrico Dandolo and dominated Mediterranean commerce for centuries.
swap.answerHtml: the Most Serene Republic of Venice [or Venezia, or La Serenissimà]
swap.answer: the Most Serene Republic of Venice
swap.clue: This republic's leaders participated in the annual "Marriage of the Sea" ceremony using the ceremonial raft Bucentaur.

question.leadin: In 415 BCE, an expedition of over 100 triremes [tri-reems] sailed to this island to attack the city of Syracuse.
question.text: Name this island off the coast of Italy.
question.clue: It's not Cilicia ("sih-LICK-ee-uh"), but early Greek colonists founded this region's cities of Selinus ("seh-LEE-nus"), Leontini ("lee-on-TEE-nee"), and Gela ("GEH-luh").

swap.leadin: While in exile, this man fought in Uruguay.
swap.text: Name this revolutionary who led the redshirts of the Expedition of the Thousand against the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.
swap.clue: He was once offered command on the Union side of the Civil War, and one campaign by this man began at Marsala.

question.leadin: Answer the following about things named Barbarossa.
question.text: Andrea Doria, an admiral from this maritime rival city of Venice, led the Holy League when it was defeated by Hayreddin Barbarossa at the Battle of Preveza.
question.answerHtml: Genoa [or Genova; or Genua; or the Republic of Genoa; or Reppublica di Genova; or Repubrica de Zena]
question.clue: A territory ruled by this city was attacked in 1553 by a joint Franco-Ottoman force under Turgut Reis.

swap.leadin: The French won a victory at Agnadello while acting as a member of this alliance.
swap.text: Name this alliance named for a city in France, formed by France, Aragon, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Papacy against the aggression of a certain Italian city.
swap.clue: Its opponent blamed the defeat on the indecisive leadership of Leonardo Loredan, which was thought to have contributed to the loss at Agnadello.

question.text: This grandfather of Lorenzo de Medici was a skillful statesman during the Italian Renaissance, doing things like keeping councillors in the Florentine Signoria loyal to him. He was succeeded by his son, Piero.
question.clue: This man persuaded Pope Eugene IV to move the Council of Ferrara to his city, thereby attracting Byzantine wealth and learning.

swap.text: The most infamous incident in the Years of Lead was the kidnapping and assassination of this Prime Minister of Italy by the Red Brigades terrorist group.
swap.clue: Inspector Leonardi was in charge of this man's protection, though his warnings about insufficiency of forces were ignored.

question.leadin: The cristallo produced in this city was the first completely transparent form of glass ever manufactured.
question.text: Name this city, whose island of Murano was long a hub for glassmaking.
question.clue: Its first patron saint was Theodore, but in 828 it obtained the relics of Saint Mark.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the reign of Spanish king Charles I.
swap.text: At this 1525 battle in northern Italy, Charles' forces recaptured Milan and took Francis I of France as prisoner.
swap.clue: The final active Yorkist pretender to the English throne, Richard de la Pole, was killed at this battle.

question.leadin: This group sparked the victory of Victor Emmanuel II over Francis II of the Two Sicilies.
question.text: Name this Italian Risorgimento group, also known as the Thousand, which took its name from its uniformly colored clothing.
question.clue: Nino Bixio repressed revolts in various regions by leading this group, whose leader gave up political leadership at the Bridge of Teano.

swap.text: In Italy, the violent period from the late 1960s to the early 1980s is known by this name. It included a bombing of a train station in Bologna.
swap.clue: This period was preceded by a series of violent strikes known as the Hot Autumn.

question.leadin: Name these influential works of pre-modern Italy.
question.text: This monumental epic poem has Dante journey through the Inferno, Purgatory, and Paradise.

swap.text: Supported by Charles Emmanuel III, Rosa Govone organized a convitti consisting of a series of shelters and textile shops to provide work to young women throughout this duchy. Monarchs of Italy following the 19th-century reunification came from a family named for this duchy's namesake county, who ruled Piedmont-Sardinia.
swap.answerHtml: Duchy of Savoy [or Duché de Savoie or Ducato di Savoia; accept County of Savoy; accept House of Savoy or Savoyards]
swap.clue: That duke of this region married his son to the sister of Louis XIII, Christine Marie.

question.leadin: This man's body was found over two months after he had got into a Lancia Lambda on the Tiber embankment with some murderous fascists.
question.text: Name this Italian socialist politician who was kidnapped and repeatedly stabbed with a carpenter's file after he delivered a speech criticising the impact of the Acerbo Law on elections.
question.clue: In his book The Fascisti Exposed, what socialist politician claimed the 1924 general election to be fraudulent? This fierce opponent of fascism was later kidnapped and murdered, triggering a namesake crisis.

swap.leadin: This man, who created 28 alberghi ("all-BAIR-ghee") clans, fought against the French in their invasion of Corsica.
swap.text: Name this statesman who, at the Battle of Preveza, withdrew after Hayreddin Barbarossa took thousands of his men prisoner. This man regretted joining Charles V on his 1541 Algiers expedition.
swap.clue: This man was made Prince of Melfi by Holy Roman Emperor Charles V after betraying Francis I during the Siege of Naples.

question.text: Mussolini's government used this two-word expression to refer to the Libyan coast, where it settled 100,000 Italian peasants. This phrase evoked Italian irredentist ambitions to dominate the Mediterranean, which they called "Mare Nostrum."
question.clue: In another story of Italian conquest, d'Annunzio (duh-NOON-zee-oh) and Mussolini referred to Italian Libya as this geographical feature, referring to the fact that it was the Italian empire's southernmost border on the Mediterranean.

swap.text: In 1805, Napoleon had this ancient object - dating back to a certain Dark Age tribe - placed on his head, thereby declaring himself King of Italy.
swap.clue: By the reign of Henry VII in the 14th century, it was traditional for the Holy Roman Emperor to also be crowned King of Italy in Milan using this object, which supposedly contained a nail from the True Cross.

question.leadin: How much do you really know about the Treaty of Utrecht? Answer, FTPE.
question.text: This Italian state and ally of England received Sicily.
question.clue: Davies listed this region as one of the title places in his Vanished Kingdoms, in which he called this place the "House that Humbert Built." This region gives its name to the family to which the kings of unified Italy belonged.

swap.leadin: King Charles Robert I of this dynasty appears on the 200 Forint bill in Hungary, which he ruled from 1312 to 1342.
swap.text: Name this royal house from the namesake area of France, who descend from a younger son of Blanche of Castile and more notably ruled Sicily and Naples.
swap.clue: In 1460, Skanderbeg led an expedition to help Ferdinand I of Naples defend against this house. A member of this house, Charles II, defended against the House of Barcelona in the War of the Sicilian Vespers.
